title: Diagnosing GNN Failure Modeswith Layer-Wise Probe Entropy

paper.title: Diagnosing GNN Failure Modes with Layer-Wise Probe Entropy
paper.abstract: Abstract Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically evaluated only at their final layer, obscuring how task-relevant information evolves during message passing. We introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that freezes a trained GNN, fits an independent linear probe to each layer, and tracks probe accuracy alongside normalized predictive entropy. Across real and synthetic graph settings, layer-wise probe entropy distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, a capability not demonstrated by existing geometric measures. Moreover, by comparing shallow and deep models, we show that the onset of entropy degradation separates the two main GNN failure modes: structural mismatch under heterophily, which appears from the earliest layers even in shallow models, and excessive-depth oversmoothing, which emerges only as propagation depth increases. These results establish probe-entropy trajectories as a tool for analyzing information flow in GNNs and motivate future work on adaptive depth selection and early-exit mechanisms.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Message-passing GNNs update node representations by aggregating information from neighbouring nodes [ 1 , 2 ] . Across layers, task-relevant information may accumulate, remain stable, or degrade. Two distinct failure modes can cause this degradation. First, excessive propagation can oversmooth representations and erase discriminative information [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Second, structural mismatch can arise under heterophily, where low-pass aggregation can mix incompatible label signals and become harmful from the first layers [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . A drop in final-layer accuracy can reveal that a failure has occurred, but it cannot distinguish between these cases. This distinction is important because the two failures require different remedies: oversmoothing may be addressed by limiting propagation depth, whereas structural mismatch may require changing the aggregation operator. Existing approaches to identifying the source of failure have largely focused on detecting oversmoothing through changes in representation geometry [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 6 ] . These measures show that representations are becoming smoother, but changes in these smoothness measures alone do not establish whether smoothing improves, preserves, or degrades task performance. When smoothing is harmful, these measures alone also cannot determine whether the failure arises from excessive-depth oversmoothing or from aggregation that is harmful from the first layers under heterophily. Recent work on sequential reasoning uses predictive entropy across intermediate steps to track how answer-relevant information evolves during computation [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . We study whether tracking entropy across GNN layers can similarly reveal how task-relevant information evolves and distinguish the two failure modes through their different trajectories: heterophily can be harmful from the first layers even in shallow models, whereas oversmoothing emerges only at greater total model depth. Concretely, we introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that tracks probe accuracy and predictive entropy across GNN layers and shows which of the two failure modes is occurring in controlled settings. Our contributions are: 1. We introduce a layer-wise probe entropy diagnostic to track how usable label information evolves during message passing. 2. We demonstrate that probe entropy trajectories distinguish beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, whereas Dirichlet energy and MAD do not consistently track these predictive consequences. 3. We show that failure onset in probe entropy trajectories across shallow and deep models helps distinguish structural mismatch from oversmoothing in controlled settings across architectures. 4. We analyze the reliability of the diagnostic across graph regimes, showing that per-node entropy-confidence alignment weakens under heterophily.

sections.heading: Failure-mode diagnostics in message-passing GNNs.
sections.text: Message-passing GNNs are subject to two main failure modes. The first is oversmoothing, a depth-related failure in which repeated message passing makes node representations increasingly similar and removes class-discriminative information [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Oversmoothing is commonly diagnosed by tracking geometric quantities across layers: MAD measures distances between node representations [ 10 ] , while Dirichlet energy measures feature variation across graph edges [ 11 , 12 ] . These establish that smoothing occurs, but not its predictive consequence: whether it helps or harms task performance. Rank-based diagnostics track collapse more directly, with rank drops aligning with performance degradation [ 16 ] . However, the dependence of rank on representation dimension complicates direct comparisons across layers. The group distance ratio R Group R_{\mathrm{Group}} [ 17 ] instead compares inter-group to intra-group distances among node representations, but requires labels for the evaluated nodes. These diagnostics describe representation geometry and class separation. We complement them with layer-wise probe entropy, which tracks predictive uncertainty through a linear probe fitted at each layer. The second failure mode arises under heterophily: low-pass aggregation can mix incompatible label signals and become harmful from the first message-passing layer, reflecting a structural mismatch between the aggregation operator and the task [ 7 , 8 ] . Heterophily-aware architectures such as H2GCN and GPR-GNN [ 8 , 18 ] mitigate this mismatch but do not diagnose post hoc whether it has occurred in a trained model. A drop in final-layer accuracy can reveal that message passing has failed, but it cannot distinguish oversmoothing from structural mismatch [ 9 ] . We address this gap by comparing the onset of entropy degradation between a shallow and a deeper model, alongside probe accuracy, to help distinguish the two failure modes.

sections.heading: Layer-wise probing methods.
sections.text: Layer-wise probing provides a task-aware way to inspect intermediate representations. It freezes the model and fits an auxiliary classifier at each layer to measure how readily task labels can be decoded [ 19 ] . This approach has also been applied to graph models. For example, [ 20 ] uses probes at different layers to recover chemical and structural properties, while [ 21 ] examines how graph-theoretic properties are represented across GNN layers. We instead use layer-wise probe entropy to assess whether smoothing improves, preserves, or degrades label readability, and to distinguish message-passing failure modes.

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate whether layer-wise probe entropy can distinguish the predictive consequences of smoothing and the failure modes underlying harmful message passing. Our experiments span 12 real-world datasets, controlled homophily settings, multiple model depths, and both GCN and GAT. We seek to address the following questions: (Q1) Can layer-wise probe entropy reveal whether smoothing is beneficial, neutral, or harmful? (Q2) Can failure onset in probe entropy trajectories distinguish structural mismatch from excessive-depth oversmoothing? Complete experimental settings and dataset details are provided in Appendix A . Additional experiments are presented in Appendix B , with supporting analyses in Appendix C .

sections.heading: (A1) Probe entropy trajectories distinguish beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing.
sections.text: On Cora, message passing increases probe accuracy and lowers probe entropy. Amazon-Ratings, shown in the middle row of Figure 1 , exhibits a neutral response. On Roman-Empire, message passing decreases accuracy and raises entropy. Dirichlet energy decreases sharply in all three cases, while MAD changes substantially but non-uniformly. Therefore, neither Dirichlet energy nor MAD identifies whether smoothing is beneficial, neutral, or harmful. After averaging input-to-final-layer changes over five runs per setting, we correlate diagnostic changes with probe-accuracy changes. sections.heading: 4.2 Failure-Onset Signatures Enable Failure-Mode Detection
sections.text: To answer Q2 , we use GraphUniverse [ 22 ] to generate controlled graphs at different homophily levels and independently train models at multiple total depths. Varying homophily controls structural mismatch between graph aggregation and label structure, while varying total depth allows us to study excessive-depth oversmoothing.

sections.heading:
(A2) Failure onset in probe entropy trajectories distinguishes
structural mismatch from oversmoothing.
sections.text: Failure onset refers to whether a harmful entropy increase appears immediately even in a shallow model or emerges only when the model becomes deep. Figure 2 compares these patterns. Under low homophily, entropy rises from the first message-passing layer in both the D = 4 D=4 and D = 10 D=10 models, accompanied by an accuracy drop. This immediate pattern across model depths indicates structural mismatch. Under high homophily, the shallow model improves accuracy and lowers entropy, whereas entropy rises from the first layer and remains high through most intermediate layers in the deep model. The depth grid also provides evidence of excessive-depth oversmoothing: beyond the shallow optimum, final accuracy decreases while final-layer entropy increases. The same patterns persist across eight model depths and both GCN and GAT. Complete controlled results and illustrative real-data trajectories on Cora and Roman-Empire are provided in Appendix B.2 . sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: Probe entropy measures the concentration of the predictive distribution rather than whether the prediction is correct. Confident predictions may therefore have low entropy even when they are wrong [ 23 , 13 ] . In our experiments, aggregate entropy trajectories track changes in probe accuracy, but node-level alignment between entropy and confidence in the true class weakens under heterophily. Here, alignment is measured by the per-node Spearman correlation across layers between probe entropy and the negative log-probability assigned to the true class. Table 2 shows this pattern for both GCN and GAT at four and ten layers. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We introduced layer-wise probe entropy as a post-hoc diagnostic of message passing. It distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, which Dirichlet energy and MAD alone do not reliably distinguish in our experiments. Comparing the onset of predictive degradation across shallow and deep models helps distinguish structural mismatch from excessive-depth oversmoothing in controlled settings. As future work, the diagnostic should be evaluated across broader message-passing architectures and graph-learning tasks, as our experiments focus on GCN and GAT for node classification. Since our input, hidden, and output representations differ in dimension, we leave controlled comparisons with rank-based diagnostics at fixed representation dimension across model depths to future work. A particularly exciting consequence of our findings is the potential for entropy trajectories to guide adaptive computation, for example by selecting the propagation depth at which entropy stops decreasing or enabling early exit once entropy is sufficiently low. Another direction is to train probes online alongside the GNN, using stop-gradient connections to prevent probe losses from updating the GNN, and assess their ability to track evolving representations during training.

sections.heading: Datasets and splits.
sections.text: We evaluate 12 multiclass node-classification benchmarks spanning a broad range of graph structures. These include the Planetoid citation networks Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed [ 24 ] , the Amazon and Coauthor benchmarks [ 25 ] , WikiCS [ 26 ] , and the heterophily benchmarks Amazon-Ratings, Chameleon, Squirrel, and Roman-Empire [ 27 ] . Adjusted homophily h adj h_{\mathrm{adj}} is computed following [ 28 ] . For the controlled experiments, we generate graphs using GraphUniverse [ 22 ] , with 500 nodes and 10 classes. The high-, intermediate-, and low-homophily conditions have measured edge homophily 0.865 0.865 , 0.512 0.512 , and 0.110 0.110 , respectively, and use a fixed 60/20/20 train-validation-test split. Real-dataset statistics and split protocols are summarized in Table 3 . For Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed, the class-balanced splits additionally contain 500 validation and 1,000 test nodes. For datasets with multiple splits, split i i is paired with model run i i . Planetoid features are used without additional normalization, while Amazon and Coauthor features follow the standard benchmark preprocessing. sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: To address Q1, we train four-layer GCNs and GATs on all 12 real-world datasets. To address Q2, we train both architectures on controlled graphs at depths D ∈ { 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 , 12 , 16 , 20 } D\in\{2,4,6,8,10,12,16,20\} . We additionally use four- and ten-layer models for the node-level entropy–confidence analysis. GCN uses symmetrically normalized adjacency and 32-dimensional hidden representations. GAT uses four attention heads with eight dimensions per head, giving the same total hidden dimensionality. Both architectures use ReLU activations and are trained for 100 epochs with Adam and a learning rate of 0.01 0.01 .

sections.heading: Linear probes.
sections.text: For each input and message-passing representation, we train the independent linear probe described in Section 3 for 100 epochs after freezing the GNN. Probes are fitted on the training nodes and evaluated on the test nodes.

sections.heading: Sensitivity of DE and MAD to endpoint parameterization.
sections.text: Because Dirichlet energy and MAD can approach zero after message passing, their relative changes may concentrate near − 1 -1 , compressing differences across settings. We therefore average the endpoint ratios across the five runs within each setting and take the logarithm of the resulting 24 mean ratios. Using the same dataset-cluster bootstrap protocol, the Pearson associations remain weak for scale-normalized Dirichlet energy ( r = − 0.05 r=-0.05 , 95% CI [ − 0.38 , 0.16 ] [-0.38,0.16] ) and MAD ( r = 0.15 r=0.15 , 95% CI [ − 0.44 , 0.68 ] [-0.44,0.68] ). Because the logarithm preserves the ordering of the setting-level values, the Spearman correlations and their confidence intervals remain unchanged ( ρ = − 0.27 \rho=-0.27 and 0.17 0.17 , respectively). Thus, the observed associations for DE and MAD remain weak under the log-ratio parameterization.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.22595v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026 Diagnosing GNN Failure Modes with Layer-Wise Probe Entropy Shanzi Bao Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: sb2832@cl.cam.ac.uk Mar Gonzàlez I Català Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: mg2211@cl.cam.ac.uk Pietro Liò Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: pl219@cl.cam.ac.uk Abstract Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically evaluated only at their final layer, obscuring how task-relevant information evolves during message passing. We introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that freezes a trained GNN, fits an independent linear probe to each layer, and tracks probe accuracy alongside normalized predictive entropy. Across real and synthetic graph settings, layer-wise probe entropy distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, a capability not demonstrated by existing geometric measures. Moreover, by comparing shallow and deep models, we show that the onset of entropy degradation separates the two main GNN failure modes: structural mismatch under heterophily, which appears from the earliest layers even in shallow models, and excessive-depth oversmoothing, which emerges only as propagation depth increases. These results establish probe-entropy trajectories as a tool for analyzing information flow in GNNs and motivate future work on adaptive depth selection and early-exit mechanisms. 1 Introduction Message-passing GNNs update node representations by aggregating information from neighbouring nodes [ 1 , 2 ] . Across layers, task-relevant information may accumulate, remain stable, or degrade. Two distinct failure modes can cause this degradation. First, excessive propagation can oversmooth representations and erase discriminative information [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Second, structural mismatch can arise under heterophily, where low-pass aggregation can mix incompatible label signals and become harmful from the first layers [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . A drop in final-layer accuracy can reveal that a failure has occurred, but it cannot distinguish between these cases. This distinction is important because the two failures require different remedies: oversmoothing may be addressed by limiting propagation depth, whereas structural mismatch may require changing the aggregation operator. Existing approaches to identifying the source of failure have largely focused on detecting oversmoothing through changes in representation geometry [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 6 ] . These measures show that representations are becoming smoother, but changes in these smoothness measures alone do not establish whether smoothing improves, preserves, or degrades task performance. When smoothing is harmful, these measures alone also cannot determine whether the failure arises from excessive-depth oversmoothing or from aggregation that is harmful from the first layers under heterophily. Recent work on sequential reasoning uses predictive entropy across intermediate steps to track how answer-relevant information evolves during computation [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . We study whether tracking entropy across GNN layers can similarly reveal how task-relevant information evolves and distinguish the two failure modes through their different trajectories: heterophily can be harmful from the first layers even in shallow models, whereas oversmoothing emerges only at greater total model depth. Concretely, we introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that tracks probe accuracy and predictive entropy across GNN layers and shows which of the two failure modes is occurring in controlled settings. Our contributions are: 1. We introduce a layer-wise probe entropy diagnostic to track how usable label information evolves during message passing. 2. We demonstrate that probe entropy trajectories distinguish beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, whereas Dirichlet energy and MAD do not consistently track these predictive consequences. 3. We show that failure onset in probe entropy trajectories across shallow and deep models helps distinguish structural mismatch from oversmoothing in controlled settings across architectures. 4. We analyze the reliability of the diagnostic across graph regimes, showing that per-node entropy-confidence alignment weakens under heterophily. 2 Related Work Failure-mode diagnostics in message-passing GNNs. Message-passing GNNs are subject to two main failure modes. The first is oversmoothing, a depth-related failure in which repeated message passing makes node representations increasingly similar and removes class-discriminative information [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Oversmoothing is commonly diagnosed by tracking geometric quantities across layers: MAD measures distances between node representations [ 10 ] , while Dirichlet energy measures feature variation across graph edges [ 11 , 12 ] . These establish that smoothing occurs, but not its predictive consequence: whether it helps or harms task performance. Rank-based diagnostics track collapse more directly, with rank drops aligning with performance degradation [ 16 ] . However, the dependence of rank on representation dimension complicates direct comparisons across layers. The group distance ratio R Group R_{\mathrm{Group}} [ 17 ] instead compares inter-group to intra-group distances among node representations, but requires labels for the evaluated nodes. These diagnostics describe representation geometry and class separation. We complement them with layer-wise probe entropy, which tracks predictive uncertainty through a linear probe fitted at each layer. The second failure mode arises under heterophily: low-pass aggregation can mix incompatible label signals and become harmful from the first message-passing layer, reflecting a structural mismatch between the aggregation operator and the task [ 7 , 8 ] . Heterophily-aware architectures such as H2GCN and GPR-GNN [ 8 , 18 ] mitigate this mismatch but do not diagnose post hoc whether it has occurred in a trained model. A drop in final-layer accuracy can reveal that message passing has failed, but it cannot distinguish oversmoothing from structural mismatch [ 9 ] . We address this gap by comparing the onset of entropy degradation between a shallow and a deeper model, alongside probe accuracy, to help distinguish the two failure modes. Layer-wise probing methods. Layer-wise probing provides a task-aware way to inspect intermediate representations. It freezes the model and fits an auxiliary classifier at each layer to measure how readily task labels can be decoded [ 19 ] . This approach has also been applied to graph models. For example, [ 20 ] uses probes at different layers to recover chemical and structural properties, while [ 21 ] examines how graph-theoretic properties are represented across GNN layers. We instead use layer-wise probe entropy to assess whether smoothing improves, preserves, or degrades label readability, and to distinguish message-passing failure modes. 3 Layer-Wise Probe Entropy After training, we freeze the GNN and fit an independent linear probe to each layer, including the input representation, using the labelled training nodes. Definition 1 (Normalized probe entropy) Given a node v v and layer k k , let h v ( k ) h_{v}^{(k)} be the node representation, p ( k ) ​ ( y ∣ h v ( k ) ) p^{(k)}(y\mid h_{v}^{(k)}) be the probe’s categorical distribution over the class label y y , p c ( k ) ​ ( v ) p_{c}^{(k)}(v) be the predicted probability that node v v belongs to class c c and C C be the number of classes. Then normalized probe entropy is defined as H ~ k ( v ) = − 1 log ⁡ C ∑ c = 1 C p c ( k ) ( v ) log p c ( k ) ( v ) . \widetilde{H}_{k}(v)=-\frac{1}{\log C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}p_{c}^{(k)}(v)\log p_{c}^{(k)}(v). For layer k k , we report the probe accuracy A k A_{k} and the mean entropy over the test-node set 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , H ¯ k = 1 | 𝒯 | ​ ∑ v ∈ 𝒯 H ~ k ​ ( v ) , \overline{H}_{k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{H}_{k}(v), where | 𝒯 | |\mathcal{T}| is the number of test nodes. Both quantities are summarized across independent runs. We use probe accuracy to validate entropy as a diagnostic; once the probes are trained, entropy can be computed for any evaluation node without access to its label. 4 Results In this section, we evaluate whether layer-wise probe entropy can distinguish the predictive consequences of smoothing and the failure modes underlying harmful message passing. Our experiments span 12 real-world datasets, controlled homophily settings, multiple model depths, and both GCN and GAT. We seek to address the following questions: (Q1) Can layer-wise probe entropy reveal whether smoothing is beneficial, neutral, or harmful? (Q2) Can failure onset in probe entropy trajectories distinguish structural mismatch from excessive-depth oversmoothing? Complete experimental settings and dataset details are provided in Appendix A . Additional experiments are presented in Appendix B , with supporting analyses in Appendix C . 4.1 Beneficial, Neutral, and Harmful Smoothing Figure 1 answers Q1 by comparing probe entropy and geometric trajectories under beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing. Therefore, neither Dirichlet energy nor MAD identifies whether smoothing is beneficial, neutral, or harmful. Varying homophily controls structural mismatch between graph aggregation and label structure, while varying total depth allows us to study excessive-depth oversmoothing. (A2) Failure onset in probe entropy trajectories distinguishes structural mismatch from oversmoothing. Failure onset refers to whether a harmful entropy increase appears immediately even in a shallow model or emerges only when the model becomes deep. Figure 2 compares these patterns. Under low homophily, entropy rises from the first message-passing layer in both the D = 4 D=4 and D = 10 D=10 models, accompanied by an accuracy drop. This immediate pattern across model depths indicates structural mismatch. Under high homophily, the shallow model improves accuracy and lowers entropy, whereas entropy rises from the first layer and remains high through most intermediate layers in the deep model. The depth grid also provides evidence of excessive-depth oversmoothing: beyond the shallow optimum, final accuracy decreases while final-layer entropy increases. Confident predictions may therefore have low entropy even when they are wrong [ 23 , 13 ] . In our experiments, aggregate entropy trajectories track changes in probe accuracy, but node-level alignment between entropy and confidence in the true class weakens under heterophily. It distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, which Dirichlet energy and MAD alone do not reliably distinguish in our experiments. Comparing the onset of predictive degradation across shallow and deep models helps distinguish structural mismatch from excessive-depth oversmoothing in controlled settings. As future work, the diagnostic should be evaluated across broader message-passing architectures and graph-learning tasks, as our experiments focus on GCN and GAT for node classification. Since our input, hidden, and output representations differ in dimension, we leave controlled comparisons with rank-based diagnostics at fixed representation dimension across model depths to future work. A particularly exciting consequence of our findings is the potential for entropy trajectories to guide adaptive computation, for example by selecting the propagation depth at which entropy stops decreasing or enabling early exit once entropy is sufficiently low. Another direction is to train probes online alongside the GNN, using stop-gradient connections to prevent probe losses from updating the GNN, and assess their ability to track evolving representations during training.
